newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks demand time to probe Holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks demand time to probe Holocaust claims.

text.p: Swiss bankers on Thursday demanded more time to probe fresh accusations that they deliberately stonewalled families of Holocaust victims who had deposited wealth in Switzerland before the Nazis exterminated them.

Rocked by new attacks at a U.S. Senate hearing in New York, the Swiss Bankers Association (SBV) insisted banks and officials were doing their utmost to clear up the claims that have drawn international attention.
"We have already started and now it is a matter of letting us get down to work," said SBV spokeswoman Sylvia Matile.

Alfonse D'Amato, powerful head of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, on Wednesday charged that Switzerland "blatantly benefitted from the Holocaust" and said the Swiss government secretly used Jewish assets to compensate its own citizens.

At the hearing, Holocaust survivors wept while recalling their ordeal trying to persuade Swiss banks to hand back murdered relatives' wealth. They said some banks demanded death certificates for account holders who perished in death camps.

D'Amato also said researchers had found documents showing the Swiss made secret deals with Poland, Hungary and Czechoslavakia to use the assets of Eastern European Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by communist regimes in the region.
Swiss foreign ministry officials were not available to comment on the accusation.
Matile noted that Switzerland was active on three levels to search for any lost Holocaust accounts.
For one thing, a banking ombudsman is helping individuals try to track down missing accounts.
"He is making it easier to avoid such cases in the future, to facilitate searches so that one no longer demands death certificates, for example, or such things," Matile said.

A separate independent panel agreed by the SBV and Jewish groups in May and headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker is also examining whether banks did all they could to locate Holocaust victims' accounts.

Parliament is set to give final approval in December to a panel of experts empowered to lift strict banking secrecy and conduct a sweeping five-year review of Swiss financial links to the Nazis and review the fate of Nazi victims' wealth.
"We hope and we expect these these three fields of activity will deal with this difficult problem in a comprehensive way," Matile said.
"One should take the different reports and look at the results. We have to live with the result no matter how it appears. It may be less spectacular than some people expect."
Matile said it was too soon to say whether the publicity surrounding the search for Holocaust accounts would leave permanent scars on Switzerland's reputation as a banking centre.

"We do not at this stage see any signs of concrete damage. It is possible this will have an effect over time, but it is hard to judge. What is difficult is that we are doing everything conceivable and we think one should let us get down to work."

Swiss banks have never disputed they were a popular refuge for the wealth of European Jews fearing Nazi persecution after Hitler came to power in Germany in 1933. Many were drawn by Switzerland's strict bank secrecy and neutral status.

But the banks reject claims by the World Jewish Congress that they may be sitting on billions of dollars in assets left behind by Jewish account holders murdered in the Holocaust without having passed along their secret bank details.
